tip: 'Zwischen' takes the dative for a fixed position, which is why 'Stuhl' becomes the dative plural 'Stühlen'.
'Warten' pairs with 'auf' plus the accusative to mean to wait for: 'warten auf unsere Freunde'.
'Über' takes the accusative when there is movement across: 'ich fahre über die Brücke'.
'Sich wohlfühlen' needs the reflexive pronoun: 'ich fühle mich ... wohl' means I feel comfortable.
Add '-in' to make a job title feminine: 'Astronom' becomes 'Astronomin' for a female astronomer.
'Neben' takes the dative for a static position: 'neben ihrem Freund' shows where she is sitting.
Tomorrow morning is 'morgen früh', not 'morgen Morgen'.
'Stehen' plus a dative person means to suit someone: 'die blaue Jacke steht dir gut'.
The passive is 'werden' plus a past participle: 'werden ... bekannt gegeben' means are announced.
'Sich entscheiden für' means to decide on and takes the accusative: 'für den Fortgeschrittenenkurs'.
For actions on your own body, German uses a dative pronoun plus 'der/die/das', not a possessive: 'ich putze mir ... die Zähne'.
Borrowed English nouns often become neuter: 'das Notebook', 'das Update'.
'Interesse' pairs with 'an' to mean interest in: 'Interesse an Kunstgeschichte'.
To say much better, put 'viel' before the comparative: 'viel besser'.
With 'seit', German uses the present tense where English uses have been: 'ich bin seit einer Stunde hier'.
Many short adjectives add an umlaut in the comparative: 'gesund' becomes 'gesünder'.
German says the units before the tens: 'dreiundfünfzig' is three-and-fifty, 53.
The formal command keeps 'Sie' right after the verb, same order as a question: 'schalten Sie bitte ...' = please switch.
An infinitive clause uses 'zu' plus the verb at the end, after a comma: 'zu unterschreiben'.
'Beim' plus a capitalized infinitive means while doing something: 'beim Fußballspielen' means while playing football.
'Ich wünschte' plus 'würde' expresses a wish that is not real: 'ich wünschte, meine Großeltern würden ... wohnen'.
When something other than the subject opens the sentence, the verb stays second and the subject follows it: 'auf keinen Fall darf man'.
'Dürfen' plus 'nicht' means must not or is not allowed to: 'darf ... nicht berühren'.
Use 'als' for 'than' in comparisons: 'fließender ... als' = more fluently than. 'Wie' is only for 'as...as' equality.
With a reflexive pronoun, 'sich verstehen' means get along, not understand: 'wir verstehen uns ... gut' = we get along well.
'Lassen' plus an infinitive means to have something done: 'wir lassen uns ... beraten' = we have them advise us.
German uses the 24-hour clock in schedules: 'dreizehn Uhr' is 1 pm.
Language names are capitalized and normally used without an article: 'Englisch und Französisch'.
'Dass' sends the conjugated verb to the very end of its clause: 'dass die Aufgabe schwierig ist'.
'Sich beschäftigen mit' means to occupy oneself with and takes the dative: 'mit der Planung'.
